intros.market: Five CAs control 88.8% of all WebPKI issuance, led by Internet Security Research Group at 32.6% and Google Trust Services at 21.0%. The CR3 concentration stands at 71.4%, indicating a highly consolidated market where three organizations have effective veto power over internet encryption standards. Despite 88 trusted CAs competing for the remaining 11.2% of issuance, the top two alone command over half of all certificates issued globally.
intros.trust: 335 root certificates exist across Chrome, Mozilla, Apple, and Microsoft trust stores, but only 90 roots appear in all four stores simultaneously. Microsoft maintains 142 roots not trusted by Chrome, Mozilla, or Apple, creating operational fragmentation where certificate chains valid in Edge may fail in other browsers. Only 38 CA organizations have achieved inclusion in all four root programs, reflecting the difficulty of maintaining universal trust while the stores increasingly diverge on membership decisions.
intros.conc: The WebPKI's HHI of 2015 places it in moderately concentrated territory, but the top three CAs controlling 71.4% of issuance creates systemic dependency that exceeds typical antitrust concerns. If any of the top two providers experienced an operational failure or distrust event, over half of the web's certificate infrastructure would require emergency replacement. This concentration has accelerated since Chrome's rise to 78.2% browser share, as the top CAs now optimize primarily for Chrome's root program rather than the broader ecosystem.
intros.tail: 74 CAs in the long tail collectively serve just 11.2% of issuance yet carry full trust store inclusion, creating asymmetric risk exposure for root programs. These smaller operators often lack the engineering resources and incident response capabilities of the top five, but a compliance failure by any tail CA triggers the same chain-of-trust revocation as a failure by Let's Encrypt or Google. Root programs must conduct oversight on 74 organizations to protect the 11.2% of traffic they serve, while the top five require equivalent scrutiny but cover 88.8%.
intros.geo: United States-incorporated CAs issue 92.75% of all certificates despite representing only 15 of 88 trusted CAs, while Europe's 44 CAs collectively serve just 7.16% of issuance. Asia-Pacific's 17 CAs account for 0.09% of global volume, revealing extreme geographic concentration that mirrors but exceeds the market concentration shown in the Market Share analysis. This US dominance means WebPKI governance outcomes are effectively determined by American corporate and regulatory priorities regardless of the international nature of the CA/B Forum.
intros.gov: 30 government-operated or state-owned CAs hold trusted status across root programs but collectively issue only 0.09% of certificates, indicating their presence serves strategic rather than commercial purposes. These CAs span jurisdictions including China, India, and several European nations where compelled access laws intersect with national security doctrine. Their minimal issuance volume provides limited visibility into operational practices while their trust store inclusion creates theoretical intercept capability for domestic traffic in their respective jurisdictions.
intros.jurisdiction: Five high-risk jurisdictions maintain trusted CAs under legal frameworks that mandate data access or permit compelled disclosure without judicial warrant: China, Russia, United Kingdom, Australia, and Hong Kong. India and Turkey present moderate risk through broader executive authority over digital infrastructure but less established compelled-access precedent. These jurisdictional risks compound the geographic concentration problem, as even CAs incorporated in lower-risk regions may operate infrastructure or hold keys in territories subject to compelled disclosure.
intros.ops: 1,715 total incidents have been disclosed across 55 CAs since systematic tracking began, with misissuance accounting for 658 cases and governance failures contributing 555. Self-detection accounts for only 30% of discoveries, while external researchers find 17% and automated tools catch 15%, revealing CAs systematically fail to identify their own compliance breakdowns. The 230 policy failures and 157 disclosure failures indicate operational discipline problems extend beyond technical misissuance into the governance and transparency domain covered in the Distrust History analysis.
intros.crypto: Root certificate cryptographic posture has consolidated around RSA 2048-bit and RSA 4096-bit keys with SHA-256 signatures, meeting current browser requirements but creating transition risk as post-quantum deadlines approach. The 90 roots trusted across all four stores use algorithms dating to pre-2010 standardization, while newer ECDSA roots show fragmented adoption with only partial trust store inclusion. Migration to post-quantum algorithms will require coordinated root replacement across 335 certificates with divergent lifecycles, compounded by the store disagreement patterns shown in Trust Surface data.
intros.distrust: 16 total distrust events across browser history show a pattern dominated by negligent noncompliance (7 cases) and compliance/operations failures (14 cases), with three instances of willful circumvention representing the most severe posture category. Root programs provide a median 1,185-day runway between distrust announcement and enforcement, allowing time for certificate replacement but creating extended periods where known-bad CAs remain technically trusted. The 10 CAs distrusted for pattern-of-issues demonstrate that browsers respond to systemic operational failures more than isolated incidents, consistent with the 1,715 total incidents distributed across 55 CAs in the Operational Risk data.
intros.policy: 43 active TLS-issuing CAs face cascading validity period reductions under SC-081, with only 8 already operating at the 47-day readiness threshold while 5 remain above 100 days and 3 still exceed 200 days as March 2026 enforcement approaches. The compliance burden behind this transition has grown 121x since 2000 to 6,657 total obligations spanning CA/B Forum baseline requirements, four root programs, WebTrust and ETSI audit criteria, and overlapping IETF/ISO/NIST standards. 76% of these obligations carry mandatory language, yet zero ballots have passed since 2022 to rationalize this expanding surface, forcing CAs to navigate complexity growth even as operational incident rates remain high.
intros.governance: Root program oversight coverage of disclosed incidents has collapsed from 67.8% (Chrome) and 78.0% (Mozilla) in 2019 to just 18.4% (Chrome) and 9.9% (Mozilla) in 2025, with Apple at 5.4% and Microsoft at 0.0%. Chrome commented substantively on 115 of the most recent incidents while Mozilla engaged on 48, but both programs are now ignoring over 80% of the 223 bugs filed in the latest full year. Microsoft's complete absence from oversight across 2,007 bugs in the corpus leaves its 142 unique roots effectively unmonitored despite serving Edge users, creating a governance gap that corresponds directly to the operational incident rate of 1,715 total cases.
intros.community: 56 CA/B Forum members include only 21 active participants, with 35 contributing zero ballot proposals or endorsements and creating a silent majority that ratifies decisions by abstention. Sectigo leads organizational participation while Stephen Davidson has proposed 36 ballots individually, but this concentration of policy leadership in a few voices means governance outcomes reflect narrow interests rather than ecosystem-wide consensus. The zero new ballots since 2022 on compliance rationalization despite 121x obligation growth suggests the active minority has reached decision-making gridlock even as the silent majority declines to engage.
intros.audit: Auditors identified just 31% of the 429 in-scope incidents that occurred during their audit periods, meaning 298 compliance failures received clean opinions before later disclosure through self-reports or external discovery. 42 CAs show high transparency gaps between audit letter assertions and Bugzilla incident history, while 6 qualified opinions and 12 ETSI v3.5 letters indicate auditor willingness to note concerns remains rare. 62.7% of WebTrust letters and 69.5% of ETSI letters rely on CA self-reporting as primary evidence, consistent with auditors' 31% detection rate and explaining why clean letters coexist with the 1,715 total incidents shown in Operational Risk data.
